# API Contract to Client, Gateway, and MCP Architecture

**Futurescape Technologies Pvt. Ltd. | Developer architecture | 29 September 2026**

## 1\. Decision and scope

Use a **versioned API contract per service** to generate typed clients and an initial Kong route configuration. Expose a **small approved subset** of operations to AI through FastMCP. Keep gateway policy, runtime authorization, tenant isolation, business workflows, and agent instructions in explicitly owned layers. The first implementation should use oneCRM read operations and a single oneApp Work or oneSociety endpoint group as pilots before extending the pattern to every service.

The main objective is to remove handwritten request and response mapping across Next.js, Flutter, and service integrations. A valid schema and generated client reduce boilerplate and many class-of-error risks; they do **not** prove that the implementation, deployed gateway, and mobile apps are perfectly synchronized. Contract tests, regeneration checks, and compatible rollout are mandatory.

This document covers REST/OpenAPI first, with GraphQL and Protobuf lanes where those protocols are genuinely used. It is a design, not a claim that the current services already publish complete contracts.

### Architecture choices

| Approach | Cost/complexity | Fit | Decision |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Generate SDKs only; manage Kong and AI integrations manually | Lowest initial effort; route/policy drift remains | Legacy service transition | Temporary migration path |
| Generate SDKs and base Kong routing from a reviewed OpenAPI contract; selectively derive MCP adapters | Moderate CI and contract governance; reusable across products | Multi-service Kong \+ oneSSO stack | **Adopt** |
| Build a central API platform that generates every gateway policy and every agent tool automatically | High coupling and governance burden; broad AI exposure | Large, mature platform team | Defer |

## 2\. System topology and ownership

![][image1]

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  A["Service-owned contract<br/>OpenAPI / GraphQL / Proto"] --> V["Validate, diff and publish<br/>versioned artifact"]
  V --> S["Generated SDKs<br/>TypeScript / Dart / other"]
  V --> K["Base Kong routes<br/>decK conversion"]
  V --> M["Reviewed MCP projection<br/>FastMCP allowlist"]
  P["Platform-owned policies<br/>auth, limits, CORS, telemetry"] --> K
  K --> G["Kong OSS"]
  S --> G
  M --> G
  G --> B["Service implementation<br/>tenant authorization + data"]
  I["oneSSO / Keycloak"] --> G
  I --> M
```

&nbsp;

| Owner | Source and duty | Must not be inferred solely from schema |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Service team | Contract, stable `operationId`, schemas, documented errors, implementation, provider tests | Correct tenant lookup, RBAC, idempotent mutations |
| Platform/API team | Contract rules, generator versions, base routing merge, policy overlays, decK deployment | OneSSO validation, issuer/audience checks, key rotation, rate limits |
| Client team | Generated package consumption, thin auth/transport adapter, UX error handling | Token acquisition, retry policy, cache invalidation, offline behavior |
| AI integration team | MCP allowlist, tool descriptions, human approval for sensitive actions, Skills resources | Agent safety, access to private data, prompt trust |

&nbsp;

Each service repository owns its canonical contract at `contracts/openapi/<service>-v1.yaml`, or an equivalent schema-first/proto path. Code-first Laravel/Node/Java/Python services may export the contract, but CI must compare the export with the reviewed artifact. Consumers pin a release or immutable digest rather than reading a mutable production `/openapi.json` at build time. The contract registry is a GitLab package or artifact with service, version, commit, and SHA-256 provenance. Keep public and internal contracts separate when disclosure differs.

## 3\. Contract standards

REST is the default boundary for oneApp, oneCRM, oneSAAS, oneHRMS, oneRevenueAI, and oneSociety via Kong. Every operation has a stable, unique `operationId`; explicit method, path, parameter location, request and response schema, error responses, and `security` requirement. Use explicit nullable/optional semantics, pagination, bounded filters, UTC timestamps with timezone, money as integer minor units plus currency where appropriate, and documented error codes. Include correlation/request ID and idempotency key semantics for mutations that may be retried. Describe bearer/OIDC authorization in OpenAPI; use real server-side enforcement.

Never put client secrets, internal upstream URLs, or private `x-kong-plugin-*` policy details in customer-distributed contracts. For routes, the `servers` block used for conversion must point to a reviewed environment-specific upstream or be transformed in the build. Publish a separate consumer-facing base URL through Kong. Define a minimal `x-futurescape` metadata extension only if standard schema fields cannot capture ownership, sensitivity, and AI eligibility; keep the AI allowlist as an independent reviewed manifest.

&nbsp;

**Compatibility policy:** additive fields and optional operations may be minor releases; removing/renaming fields, changing requiredness, response meaning, `operationId`, or auth scope needs a versioned migration. Mobile clients can remain installed long after deployment, so the backend must support the prior supported contract window. A successful TypeScript build is not a complete backward-compatibility check.

## 4\. Client generation matrix

| Contract | Client | Recommendation | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| OpenAPI | Next.js / TypeScript | `@hey-api/openapi-ts` for shared SDK/types; Orval when a product explicitly wants generated TanStack Query hooks | Choose **one** generator per client package. Pin exact version and review generated diffs. |
| OpenAPI | Flutter / Dart | OpenAPI Generator `dart-dio`, pilot serialization and nullability against actual endpoints | Wrap the generated package with a Dio interceptor for token, correlation ID and errors. |
| OpenAPI | Python / Go / Java | OpenAPI Generator client as needed | Generate only for real consumers; avoid publishing unused SDKs. |
| GraphQL | TypeScript | GraphQL Code Generator client preset from schema **and checked-in operations** | Operation types are derived from selected queries/mutations, not an invented REST endpoint list. |
| Protobuf / gRPC | Go / Java / TypeScript | Buf generation plus lint and breaking checks | Use for internal service boundaries with a proven need; browser/mobile support requires an appropriate transport such as Connect or a REST facade. |

`openapi-typescript-codegen` is not the default for new work. Standardize on the actively documented Hey API toolchain and pilot Orval separately if generated React Query hooks materially simplify a UI. Do not generate both into the same module. The exact version and generated import surface must be checked against the pinned tool version.

&nbsp;

**Illustrative local generation:**

```sh
npm install --save-dev --save-exact @hey-api/openapi-ts
npx openapi-ts -i contracts/openapi/onecrm-v1.yaml -o packages/api-clients/onecrm/src/generated
```

The CLI name `openapi-ts` is supplied by `@hey-api/openapi-ts`. Generated APIs differ by plugin/configuration; the sample `UserService.getUserById({ id: '123' })` in the request must **not** be copied without checking actual output. Application code imports from a stable hand-maintained wrapper, not from deep generated paths:

```ts
// Example boundary, illustrative; adapt to the pinned SDK output.
const crm = createOneCrmClient({
  baseUrl: runtimeConfig.kongBaseUrl,
  accessToken: () => oneSsoSession.getAccessToken(),
});
const lead = await crm.leads.getById({ leadId });
```

The wrapper owns auth injection, timeout, error normalization, and observability. Never edit generated files. In browser code, do not embed a confidential Keycloak client secret. Enforce server-only calls where data cannot be exposed to a browser token. Publish packages by contract major version (`@futurescape/onecrm-client`) and change the package version when the generated public API changes.

## 5\. Kong conversion and policy layering

Kong decK's `openapi2kong` creates Services from `servers` and Routes per `operationId`. It can emit an `openid-connect` plugin from a matching scheme, but that plugin is **Kong Enterprise only**; Futurescape currently uses Kong OSS. Therefore treat the converter output as a routing baseline, **not an automatically secure deployment**. Keep auth and other environment policies in a platform-owned decK overlay or rendered configuration. Kong recommends policy layering with `deck file add-plugin` rather than publishing plugin configuration in shared OpenAPI files.

```sh
deck file openapi2kong --spec contracts/openapi/onecrm-v1.yaml \
  --output-file build/onecrm.base.yaml --uuid-base futurescape-onecrm-v1
# Platform pipeline: add/reconcile reviewed policy, lint/diff, then deploy.
```

The pipeline must fail when conversion unexpectedly changes public route count, method, host, path, upstream, or security association. `--uuid-base` ensures stable generated IDs across builds; avoid adopting generated IDs into a live gateway before checking the migration diff. A consolidated decK state may need namespacing and environment substitutions. Never run an unreviewed `deck gateway sync` from an application MR; platform deployment promotes an approved state after diff and staging smoke tests.

### Kong OSS and oneSSO validation

Use one of two deliberately engineered paths, evaluated in a pilot:

1. **Preferred for full OIDC semantics:** a gateway-adjacent, independently deployed token validation/authorization service at the edge, with Keycloak JWKS caching and rotation, issuer, audience, expiry, not-before, allowed algorithm, scopes and tenant context checks. Restrict direct backend ingress so all public traffic traverses the edge; verify how Kong OSS calls and fails closed with this component before production.  
2. **Limited OSS baseline:** Kong OSS JWT plugin with configured Consumer public keys plus service-side issuer, audience, scope, and tenancy checks. Its basic JWT verification and selected registered claim checks are not equivalent to a complete OIDC/JWKS authorization flow; plan operational key rotation and reject unsupported token formats.

&nbsp;

In either path the backend independently enforces resource-level RBAC and tenant ownership from verified identity, not a client-supplied `societyId`, `companyId`, or request header. Strip inbound identity headers before adding trusted ones. Scope backend access to gateway/service traffic. Document machine-to-machine token exchange and audience per consuming service. Record auth failures with correlation ID, never raw bearer tokens.

## 6\. FastMCP: approved API operations, separate Skills resources

FastMCP can derive MCP tools from an OpenAPI document using `FastMCP.from_openapi(...)` and an `httpx` client. Its default converts **every operation** into a tool. That default is unacceptable for oneCRM, oneSociety accounting, payments, administration, or production actions. Build an AI-facing projection from a reviewed manifest; allowlist exact operation IDs/routes and finish the route map with `MCPType.EXCLUDE`. FastMCP route maps support explicit exclusions. Generate read-only tools first, then individually reviewed mutations. A tool description must name its scope, side effects, data sensitivity, and required authorization. Do not rely on an LLM to choose a tenant or to authorize a write.

![][image2]

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U["Agent or approved client"] --> M["MCP server<br/>auth + allowlisted tools"]
  M --> K["Kong OSS<br/>gateway policy"]
  K --> A["oneCRM API<br/>tenant and role checks"]
  M --> R["Skills resources<br/>procedural guidance"]
```

The MCP server authenticates its caller with oneSSO, maps the caller to a permitted service token using a reviewed delegation design, and forwards identity through Kong. A broad shared service token would bypass user-specific permissions and must not be used for customer data. Deny unsupported scopes, enforce per-tool limits, cap pagination and result size, redact sensitive fields, set outbound allowlisted base URLs, and log caller, operation, tenant, latency and status without secrets. For an action with financial, publishing, administrative, or destructive effect, require a separate explicit approval flow and idempotency key; the AI cannot grant itself approval. Use staging fixtures and negative authorization tests.

&nbsp;

The FastMCP **Skills Provider** serves `SKILL.md` and optional supporting files as `skill://` resources. It does not turn those instructions into an HTTP client or automatically implement endpoint permissions. Use it for approved agent playbooks such as “how to inspect a oneCRM lead safely” or “how to prepare a draft campaign,” paired with separately secured tools. Treat skill text as versioned, reviewed instructions: exclude credentials, private customer examples, executable secrets, and untrusted external skill directories. An agent needs an MCP client that can discover/read resources, and its instruction to read the relevant skill must be explicit.

For oneRevenueAI, begin with read-only oneCRM lead summaries and oneSocial campaign analytics; post creation/publishing remains mediated by oneSocial's existing approval and scheduling ownership. Do not expose raw billing, KYC, society ledger, or tenant administration operations in the first MCP release.

## 7\. CI/CD contract pipeline

![][image3]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  C["Contract MR"] --> L["Lint + resolve refs + security rules"]
  L --> D["Breaking diff vs published contract"]
  D --> G["Regenerate SDKs + compile consumers"]
  G --> T["Provider/consumer contract tests"]
  T --> R["Render Kong routes + reviewed policy"]
  R --> S["Staging deploy + auth/tenant smoke tests"]
  S --> P["Publish versioned SDK and contract"]
```

&nbsp;

**Required gates:** (1) syntax, schema references, operation ID uniqueness, documented 4xx/5xx and security scheme; (2) backward compatibility against last released contract; (3) deterministic generation with pinned tools and clean diff; (4) generated TypeScript/Dart compile and representative serialization tests; (5) provider response and error conformance using real service fixtures, including pagination and nullable fields; (6) Kong state diff, disabled unsupported plugins, negative auth tests, header spoof tests, tenant-crossing tests; (7) MCP allowlist snapshot, excluded admin routes, least-privilege and tool-call negative tests. For GraphQL, validate operations against schema and detect removed fields; for Proto, run `buf lint` and `buf breaking` against the published baseline.

**Release order:** deploy additive backend support → apply reviewed Kong state → publish SDK/package → release web app → roll out mobile app → measure old client usage → retire fields/routes after compatibility window. For a breaking change, publish `/v2` or another explicitly versioned contract and run both routes during migration. Roll back gateway and backend together using the last known good decK state; avoid changing a mobile client contract underneath installed versions.

## 8\. Pilot acceptance and rollout

| Phase | Scope | Exit evidence |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 0\. Inventory | Find existing OpenAPI/GraphQL/Proto artifacts and actual gateway routes for oneCRM and oneApp Work; map current token validation | Named owners; route-to-operation reconciliation; documented gaps |
| 1\. Contract pilot | Complete 5–10 oneCRM read operations and oneApp Work endpoint group; stable versioned contracts | CI lint/diff and provider conformance; generated TS and Dart build |
| 2\. Gateway pilot | Generate base Kong routes, merge OSS compatible policies, stage | Reviewed decK diff; denied expired/wrong-audience tokens and cross-tenant access |
| 3\. MCP pilot | Expose at most three read-only oneCRM or oneSocial operations with explicit allowlist; publish one reviewed skills resource | Authorized tool calls work; excluded routes remain absent; audit trail complete |
| 4\. Expansion | Move service by service; publish packages and contract registry | Reduced handwritten HTTP code and no unreviewed route drift |

The first delivery is accepted only when a schema change causes an automated generated-client diff; an incompatible change blocks merge; a server response violating the contract fails tests; Kong rejects invalid identity at the chosen edge layer; a valid identity cannot cross tenants; and MCP does not list or invoke non-allowlisted operations. Track generation/build failures, contract mismatch rates, auth denial reasons, route drift, MCP tool calls, and per-service migration coverage.

## 9\. Developer checklist

1. Identify the contract owner and current published version; reconcile with the implemented routes.  
2. Assign stable operation IDs and explicit auth/error schemas; document tenant context and idempotency.  
3. Pin one generator per client target; generate into a disposable directory and expose a stable wrapper.  
4. Run schema lint, compatibility diff, provider conformance, generated compile and serialization checks.  
5. Render decK route state, merge platform-owned policies, inspect gateway diff and staging tests.  
6. Confirm Kong OSS plugin availability; never deploy Enterprise OIDC config to OSS.  
7. Approve MCP tool operations one by one and verify the catch-all exclusion; keep Skills resources separately reviewed.  
8. Release backend and gateway compatibility before web/mobile client updates; record provenance and rollback state.
